pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.1.2)
- B7.1.2.1 — Apply mental mathematics strategies and number properties used to solve problems. B7.1.2.2 — Demonstrate an understanding of the addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of (i) whole numbers and (ii) decimal numbers to solve problems. B7.1.2.3 — Demonstrate understanding and the use of powers of natural numbers in solving problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- multiply and divide numbers, including decimals, by powers of 10
- use halving and doubling and the distributive property for quick mental calculation
- solve word problems mentally
- add, subtract, multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals using expanded form, place value and lattice methods
- use divisibility tests
- write numbers as products of powers and evaluate powers
- use prime factorisation to find the HCF and LCM and solve real-life problems

pages.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Multiply and divide given numbers by powers of 10 including decimals and benchmark fractions.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.1
## Basic facts
Quick recall of multiplication facts up to 12 × 12 = 144 (and the related division facts) is the foundation of all mental mathematics. For every multiplication fact there are two division facts:
9 × 12 = 108 → 108 ÷ 9 = 12 and 108 ÷ 12 = 9
> 🧪 **Activity 2.1 — Multiplication facts relay**
1. Form teams of five. Your teacher calls out a fact such as "7 × 8". The first player to say "56" correctly wins a point for the team, and must then give a related division fact ("56 ÷ 7 = 8").
2. Continue until every fact up to 12 × 12 = 144 has been used. Record the facts your team found hardest and practise them at home.
## Benchmark fractions as decimals and percentages
| **Fraction** | [[1/2]] | [[1/4]] | [[3/4]] | [[1/5]] | [[2/5]] | [[1/10]] | [[1/3]] | [[2/3]] | [[1/8]] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Decimal | 0.5 | 0.25 | 0.75 | 0.2 | 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.333… | 0.666… | 0.125 |
| Percentage | 50% | 25% | 75% | 20% | 40% | 10% | 33[[1/3]]% | 66[[2/3]]% | 12.5% |
## Moving the decimal point
> 🔑 **Key idea: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1000** — Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves every digit 1, 2 or 3 places to the **left** (the number gets bigger). Dividing by 10, 100 or 1000 — which is the same as multiplying by [[1/10]], [[1/100]] or [[1/1000]] — moves every digit 1, 2 or 3 places to the **right** (the number gets smaller).

pages.title: Mental mathematics strategies
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply mental mathematics strategies and number properties used to perform calculations.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.2
## Halving and doubling
If you halve one factor and double the other, the product does not change. Choose the factor to halve so that the other becomes a "friendly" number such as 10 or 100.
## ✏️ Example 2.2
Use halving and doubling to find a) 28 × 5 b) 125 × 4 c) 16 × 25
**Solution**
a) 28 × 5 → halve 28, double 5 → 14 × 10 = **140**
b) 125 × 4 → (125 × 2) × 2 = 250 × 2 = **500**
c) 16 × 25 → 8 × 50 → 4 × 100 = **400**
## Using the distributive property
> 🔑 **Key idea: Distributive property** — a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c. Split one factor into a friendly sum or difference, multiply each part, then add or subtract.
## ✏️ Example 2.3
Find a) 7 × 15 b) 18 × 6 c) 8 × 99
**Solution**
a) 7 × 15 = 7 × (10 + 5) = 70 + 35 = **105**
b) 18 × 6 = (20 − 2) × 6 = (20 × 6) − (2 × 6) = 120 − 12 = **108**
c) 8 × 99 = 8 × (100 − 1) = 800 − 8 = **792**

pages.title: Solving word problems mentally
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply mental mathematics strategies to solve word problems.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.1.3
Word problems use many different words for the four operations. Learn to recognise them.
| **Operation** | **Key words and phrases** |
|---|---|
| Addition (+) | plus, add, sum, total, increase by, altogether, more than |
| Subtraction (−) | minus, take away, from a number take, difference, less than, decrease by, what must be added to make… |
| Multiplication (×) | times, multiply, product, of, square, twice, what must be divided by … to give … |
| Division (÷) | divide, share, quotient, per, how many times does it go into…, what must be multiplied by … to give … |
## ✏️ Example 2.4
Mental mathematics game — answer each quickly.
a) Find the cost of three 5 kg bags of rice at GH₵2 per kg.
b) What is the cost of 1 dozen eggs at 80 pesewas each?
c) 28 × 25
d) How many 21 cm pieces can be cut from a string one metre long?
e) What fraction of a litre is 250 ml?
f) The area of a square board is 81 cm². What is its perimeter?
g) Two angles of a triangle add up to 98°. What is the size of the third angle?
h) How many minutes are there from 10:15 a.m. to noon?
i) What is 60 pesewas as a decimal of GH₵2.40?
**Solution**
a) 3 × 5 kg = 15 kg; 15 × GH₵2 = **GH₵30**
b) 12 × 80p = 960p = **GH₵9.60**
c) 28 × 25 = 7 × 100 = **700** (halve twice, double twice)
d) 100 ÷ 21 = 4 remainder 16, so **4 pieces** (16 cm is left over)
e) 250 ml ÷ 1000 ml = [[1/4]]
f) side = 9 cm (since 9 × 9 = 81); perimeter = 4 × 9 = **36 cm**
g) 180° − 98° = **82°**
h) 10:15 → 11:00 is 45 min; 11:00 → 12:00 is 60 min; total **105 minutes**
i) 0.60 ÷ 2.40 = [[1/4]] = **0.25**

pages.title: Keep going
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity 2.2 — Mental maths quiz show**
In groups, each learner writes three word problems on cards using different key words (e.g. "Increase 45 by 38", "What must be added to 67 to make 100?", "Share 96 oranges equally among 8 children"). Groups swap cards and race to answer mentally. Discuss the quickest strategy for each.

pages.title: Adding and subtracting whole numbers and decimals
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Add and subtract up to four-digit numbers (whole numbers and decimals).
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.2.1
Writing numbers in **expanded form** (partitioning) shows clearly which place values are being added or subtracted.
## ✏️ Example 2.5
Add 785 and 9,342 using expanded form.
**Solution**
|  | **Thousands** | **Hundreds** | **Tens** | **Ones** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 785 |  | 700 | 80 | 5 |
| 9,342 | 9,000 | 300 | 40 | 2 |
| Sum | 9,000 | 1,000 | 120 | 7 |
9,000 + 1,000 + 120 + 7 = **10,127**
## ✏️ Example 2.6
Add 327.6 and 54.13.
**Solution**
Write 327.6 as 327.60 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
327.60 = 300 + 20 + 7 + [[6/10]] + [[0/100]]
54.13 = 50 + 4 + [[1/10]] + [[3/100]]
Sum = 300 + 70 + 11 + [[7/10]] + [[3/100]] = **381.73**
## ✏️ Example 2.7
Subtract 7.85 from 93.6.
**Solution**
93.60 = 90 + 3 + [[6/10]] + [[0/100]] → regroup → 80 + 12 + [[15/10]] + [[10/100]]
7.85 = 7 + [[8/10]] + [[5/100]]
Difference = 80 + 5 + [[7/10]] + [[5/100]] = **85.75**
Check by adding: 85.75 + 7.85 = 93.60 ✓
> ⚠️ **Watch out!** Always line up the decimal points (or the place values) before adding or subtracting decimals. Fill empty places with zeros.

pages.title: Multiplying and dividing multi-digit numbers
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Multiply or divide multi-digit numbers by 1- and 2-digit numbers.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.2.2
## Partitioning (expanded form)
## ✏️ Example 2.8
Multiply 584 by 8, then use the result to find 4,672 ÷ 8.
**Solution**
584 × 8 = (500 + 80 + 4) × 8 = 4,000 + 640 + 32 = **4,672**
Division is the inverse of multiplication, so **4,672 ÷ 8 = 584**. By partitioning: 4,672 = 4,000 + 640 + 32, and 4,000 ÷ 8 = 500, 640 ÷ 8 = 80, 32 ÷ 8 = 4; 500 + 80 + 4 = 584.
## The vertical place value method
## ✏️ Example 2.9
Find 345 × 27 using the place value method.
**Solution**
|  | 345 |  |
|---|---|---|
| × | 27 |  |
|  | 2,415 | (345 × 7) |
| + | 6,900 | (345 × 20) |
|  | **9,315** |  |
## The lattice method
## ✏️ Example 2.10
Use the lattice method to find 345 × 27.
**Solution**
Draw a 2-by-3 lattice: write 3, 4, 5 across the top and 2, 7 down the right side. In each cell write the product of its column and row digits, tens above the diagonal and ones below. Then add along the diagonals from the bottom right, carrying where necessary.
[[fig:m7-f05]]
Figure 2.2: Lattice for 345 × 27
Reading the digits down the left and along the bottom: **345 × 27 = 9,315**.
## Using the distributive property
## ✏️ Example 2.11
Multiply 325 by 15 using the distributive property.
**Solution**
325 × 15 = 325 × (10 + 5) = (325 × 10) + (325 × 5)
= 3,250 + 1,625 = **4,875**

pages.title: Long division by a 2-digit number
pages.body:
## Long division by a 2-digit number
## ✏️ Example 2.12
Divide 9,315 by 27.
**Solution**
| Step | Working | Thinking |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 93 ÷ 27 = 3 r 12 | 3 × 27 = 81; 93 − 81 = 12 |
| 2 | bring down 1 → 121 | 121 ÷ 27 = 4 r 13 (4 × 27 = 108) |
| 3 | bring down 5 → 135 | 135 ÷ 27 = 5 r 0 (5 × 27 = 135) |
So **9,315 ÷ 27 = 345**.
## Divisibility tests
| **A number is divisible by …** | **if …** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | its last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) | 3,578 |
| 3 | the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 | 72: 7 + 2 = 9 ✓ |
| 4 | its last two digits form a number divisible by 4 | 1,316: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 ✓ |
| 5 | its last digit is 0 or 5 | 4,675 |
| 6 | it is divisible by both 2 and 3 | 312: even and 3+1+2 = 6 ✓ |
| 7 | doubling the last digit and subtracting it from the rest gives 0 or a multiple of 7 | 595: 59 − 10 = 49 ✓ |
| 8 | its last three digits form a number divisible by 8 | 5,120: 120 ÷ 8 = 15 ✓ |
| 9 | the sum of its digits is divisible by 9 | 7,326: 7+3+2+6 = 18 ✓ |
| 10 | its last digit is 0 | 8,740 |
## ✏️ Example 2.13
Test whether 595 is divisible by 3, 5 and 7.
**Solution**
By 3: 5 + 9 + 5 = 19, which is not divisible by 3 → **No**.
By 5: last digit is 5 → **Yes** (595 ÷ 5 = 119).
By 7: double the last digit: 5 × 2 = 10; 59 − 10 = 49 = 7 × 7 → **Yes** (595 ÷ 7 = 85).

pages.title: Story problems with whole numbers and decimals
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Create and solve story problems involving decimals on the four basic operations.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.2.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Solving word problems** —
1. Read the problem carefully. 2. Underline what is given and what is asked. 3. Choose the operation(s). 4. Calculate. 5. Write the answer in a sentence with the correct unit, and check that it is reasonable.
## ✏️ Example 2.14
A group of two hundred and fifteen men and seven hundred and eighty-four women went to watch a musical concert. GH₵25 was collected at the gate from each person. How much money was collected altogether?
**Solution**
Number of people = 215 + 784 = 999
Money collected = 999 × GH₵25 = (1,000 − 1) × 25 = 25,000 − 25 = **GH₵24,975**
## ✏️ Example 2.15
Mrs Adamu bought 13.6 kg of meat. Mrs Anderson bought 2.4 kg of meat less than Mrs Adamu. How many kilograms of meat did they buy altogether?
**Solution**
Mrs Anderson: 13.6 − 2.4 = 11.2 kg
Altogether: 13.6 + 11.2 = **24.8 kg**
## ✏️ Example 2.16
Ebo weighs 28.6 kg. His father is four times as heavy. What is the total weight of Ebo and his father?
**Solution**
Father: 4 × 28.6 = 114.4 kg
Total = 28.6 + 114.4 = **143.0 kg** (or 5 × 28.6 = 143 kg)
## ✏️ Example 2.17
Mrs Armah bought 45.75 metres of linen for her five children. If they share it equally, how many metres does each receive?
**Solution**
45.75 ÷ 5 = **9.15 m** each

pages.title: Example 2.18
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 2.18
A school's Management Committee approved this budget for its open day anniversary.
| **Activity** | **Cost (GH₵)** |
|---|---|
| Painting school building | 4,580 |
| Mending cracks on the basketball pitch | 3,050 |
| Restocking the library with new books | 2,690 |
| Buying choir robes | 5,340 |
| Buying prizes for awards | 4,270 |
a) How much was approved for painting the school building and buying choir robes?
b) How much more was to be spent on mending the cracks than on restocking the library?
c) How much was spent on prizes if twice the approved amount was spent on this activity?
**Solution**
a) 4,580 + 5,340 = **GH₵9,920**
b) 3,050 − 2,690 = **GH₵360**
c) 2 × 4,270 = **GH₵8,540**

pages.title: Powers of natural numbers
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Illustrate with examples the meaning of repeated factors using counting objects such as bottle tops or bundles of sticks.
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.3.1
When the same number is multiplied by itself several times, it is called a **repeated factor**. In 3 × 3 × 3 each factor is 3.
[[fig:m7-f06|Figure 2.3: Modelling 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 with bottle tops: 3 groups of (3 rows of 3)]]
> 🔑 **Key idea: Power, base and index** — A product of repeated factors can be written as a **power**. In 2^{3} (read "2 to the power 3" or "2 cubed"), 2 is the **base** and 3 is the **index** (also called the **exponent** or **power**). The index tells how many times the base is used as a factor: 2^{3} = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
## ✏️ Example 2.19
Explain the meaning of a) 2^{5} b) 10^{4} and evaluate each.
**Solution**
a) 2^{5} = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = **32**. The base is 2 and the index is 5.
b) 10^{4} = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = **10,000**. The base is 10 and the index is 4.
**Indicator B7.1.2.3.2** Express a given number as a product of a given number or numbers and in the form of a power or a product of powers.
## ✏️ Example 2.20
Express as a power or as a product of powers: a) 32 b) 81 c) 49 d) 16 × 27
**Solution**
a) 32 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^{5}
b) 81 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3^{4}
c) 49 = 7 × 7 = 7^{2}
d) 16 × 27 = (2 × 2 × 2 × 2) × (3 × 3 × 3) = 2^{4}×3^{3}

pages.title: Example 2.21
pages.body:
**Indicator B7.1.2.3.3** Show that the value of any natural number with zero as its exponent is 1 and use it to solve problems.
## ✏️ Example 2.21
Show that 2^{0} = 1 and 3^{0} = 1.
**Solution**
Any number (except 0) divided by itself is 1. Using powers:
[[2^{2}/2^{2}]] = [[2×2/2×2]] = 1
But when we divide powers of the same base we subtract the indices: 2^{2}÷2^{2} = 2^{2−2} = 2^{0}.
So 2^{0} **= 1**. In the same way 3^{3}÷3^{3} = 3^{3−3} = 3^{0} and also [[27/27]] = 1, so 3^{0} **= 1**.
In general, for any natural number x: x^{0} = 1.
**Indicator B7.1.2.3.4** Find the value of a number written in index form.
## ✏️ Example 2.22
Evaluate: a) 5^{3} b) 3^{4} c) 6^{3} d) [[1/2^{5}]] e) 7^{0} + 4^{2}
**Solution**
a) 5^{3} = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = **125**
b) 3^{4} = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 9 × 9 = **81**
c) 6^{3} = 6 × 6 × 6 = 36 × 6 = **216**
d) [[1/2^{5}]] = [[1/2×2×2×2×2]] = [[1/32]]
e) 1 + 16 = **17**

pages.title: Prime factors, HCF and LCM
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply the concept of powers of numbers (product of primes) to find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Least Common Multiple (LCM).
Curriculum indicator B7.1.2.3.5
> 🔑 **Key idea: Prime number** — A **prime number** has exactly two factors: 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …). Every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a **product of prime factors**.
## Expanding a number as a product of primes
## ✏️ Example 2.23
Express 24 and 30 as products of prime factors, in index form.
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f07]]
Figure 2.4: Factor trees for 24 and 30
24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2^{3}×3
30 = 2 × 3 × 5
## Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Least Common Multiple (LCM)
> 🔑 **Key idea: HCF and LCM from prime factors** — **HCF**: multiply the prime factors **common** to all the numbers, each with its **lowest** index. **LCM**: multiply **every** prime factor that appears, each with its **highest** index.
## ✏️ Example 2.24
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 30.
**Solution**
24 = 2^{3}×3 30 = 2 × 3 × 5
HCF: common primes are 2 and 3; lowest powers 2^{1} and 3^{1} → HCF = 2 × 3 = **6**
LCM: primes 2, 3, 5 with highest powers 2^{3}, 3, 5 → LCM = 8 × 3 × 5 = **120**
## ✏️ Example 2.25
Akweley has two pieces of paper. One piece is 24 cm wide and the other is 30 cm wide. She wants to cut both pieces into strips of equal width that are as wide as possible. How wide should she cut the strips?
**Solution**
We are **dividing** both widths into equal smaller parts (factors) that are **common** to 24 and 30, and we want the **widest** (highest) possible strips — so we need the **HCF**.
HCF of 24 and 30 = 6
Akweley should cut each strip **6 cm wide**. (The 24 cm piece gives 4 strips and the 30 cm piece gives 5 strips.)

pages.title: Example 2.26
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 2.26
Baba exercises every 12 days and Serwa every 8 days. They both exercised today. In how many days will they next exercise on the same day?
**Solution**
The events repeat (multiples), and we want the soonest (least) day that is common to both — so we need the **LCM**.
12 = 2^{2}×3 8 = 2^{3} LCM = 2^{3}×3 = 24
They will exercise together again in **24 days**.
> 🎯 **BECE tip** HCF problems usually involve cutting, sharing or grouping into the largest equal parts. LCM problems usually involve events repeating and asking when they next happen together.

pages.title: Chapter 2 summary
pages.body:
- Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000 moves digits left; dividing (multiplying by [[1/10]], [[1/100]], [[1/1000]]) moves digits right.
- Halving and doubling, and the distributive property a(b + c) = ab + ac, make mental calculation quick.
- Expanded form, the place value method and the lattice method are reliable ways to add, subtract and multiply.
- In a^{n}, a is the base and n is the index. a^{0} = 1.
- HCF = product of common primes with lowest powers; LCM = product of all primes with highest powers.
